As the cornerstone of her community, Ms. Cummins is awarded for forty years of dedicated service providing assistance to those in need as a respected owner of a business at Eastmond Corner. Her commitment to integrity, exceptional customer care, philanthropy and entrepreneurship combined with mentorship of young people has improved the socio-economic conditions of her neighbourhood.

(27) Mr. Andrew Michael Davis, J.P.
For over forty years, Andrew “Boss” Davis, a graduate of St. Leonard’s Boys School and owner of Boss Auto Repair Shop has been a strong pillar of his community. Through mentorship, employment of at-risk youth, and fostering young entrepreneurs, he has demonstrated selflessness, integrity, and community leadership. He is acknowledged for serving as a role model and invaluable asset to his neighbourhood.

(28) Mr. Hashim Delair
Mr. Delair is honoured for over twenty years of significant contributions and steadfast advocacy to support at-risk youth in St. Michael. Through his partnership with the Juvenile Liaison Scheme, he has provided school supplies, safe employment opportunities, and mentorship to improve education, foster personal growth, and promote social empowerment, thereby creating meaningful pathways and building support systems for young people facing significant challenges.

(29) Mr. Ibrahim Mohmed Yasin Desai, J.P.
Mr. Desai is recognized for his outstanding achievements in community development and volunteerism. An admired, dependable and respected leader, he has provided employment opportunities and mentorship to residents in his neighborhood that had led to their growth, empowerment and economic enfranchisement.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(30) Mr. Uwine Fernando Dominique
As a lifelong resident of the Brittons Hill and The Grotto, St. Michael, with a proud tradition of community activism and distinguished service, he is celebrated for his leadership, mentorship, and generosity, as he has created opportunities, provided employment, and supported many in his community. As a practitioner and role model he used sport, especially football, as a vehicle for recreation, unity, guidance, and transformation. For him, service is a daily practice of looking out for neighbors and building a stronger Brittons Hill community.

(31) Mrs. Sybil Angela Fiedler
Is acknowledged for a decade of fostering creativity, skill development, and entrepreneurship among person in her community. Through her mentorship, students have achieved national recognition at NICFA and some have turned their craft into viable livelihoods. Her dedication to teaching and sharing her passion has empowered others and enriched her community.

(32) Mr. Colin Recardo Forde
This pioneering Barbadian cyclist and mentor from Westbury Road, St. Michael, is honoured for his significant achievements in sport, coaching, and community development. A member of the 1968 Olympic team and co-founder of the Caribbean Cycling Federation, he has nurtured athletes, promoted cycling, and inspired young people across many sporting disciplines. His contributions to youth development and his legacy in sport are invaluable.

(33) Mr. Everton Rudolph Gilkes
Everton Gilkes has been a dedicated coach, mentor, and community leader for many years who has used sports and training programmes to nurture talent, instilled discipline, foster teamwork and inspire community pride He is honoured for his volunteerism and selfless contributions to guiding young people and adults toward productive paths as well as creating lasting opportunities for personal and professional development.

(34) Mr. Franklyn Thurston Gill, J.P.
As a sports personality, player, national football manager, administrator, and mentor, Mr. Gill has positively influenced the sporting landscape of his parish and the island. He is honoured for a lifetime of outstanding achievement in football and athletic excellence and youth engagement. His leadership and vision have elevated standards, created opportunities and left a lasting legacy of community participation in national sports development.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(35) Mr. Deon Deangelo Glasgow
Deon Glasgow is a pioneer and young community leader who is recognised for his unswerving dedication to community empowerment and youth development in Nelson Street, St. Michael. Through his business, Deonte Exquisite Lighting, he creates job opportunities for young people, organises charity events, empowers underserved youth through skill development, and supports local recreational and sports initiatives that inspire hope and unity.

(36) Mr. Carlos Winfield Goodridge
Mr. Goodridge demonstrates the power of individual action in building vibrant communities. He is honoured for his meaningful contributions to the well- being of others and willingness to assist whether volunteering in schools, supporting local charities, mentoring young people, or organising educational and recreational activities to promote health and environmental awareness and create a safer, more caring, and connected community.

(37) Mr. Rodney Orlando Grant, J.P.
Rodney Grant is honoured for over forty years of visionary leadership in community and cultural development. As Chief Executive Officer of the Pinelands Creative Workshop, he has transformed communities through the arts, empowered marginalized and at-risk families, preserved Barbados’ intangible cultural heritage, advanced cultural education and certification and navigated and negotiated territorial conflicts through family and community crisis intervention. He is the consummate community practitioner, intermediary and advocate.

(38) Mr. Kevin Adison Greaves, J.P.
A proud member of the Grazettes community, he has significantly impacted his area through sponsorships, community clean-ups, and educational support. He is recognized for his volunteerism and philanthropy, his work with Myrna Greaves Memorial Scholarship, along with his contributions to local sports.

(39) Mrs. Sophia Mechelle Greaves-Broome
For thirty years of outstanding achievements in community and youth development. Through her leadership at the Pinelands Creative Workshop and as Special Projects Director, she has managed impactful national and regional initiatives in partnership with UNDP, UNICEF, and UNESCO, to promote economic empowerment, cultural preservation, and human development that have positively transformed lives and strengthened communities in the Pine, and across Barbados and the Eastern Caribbean.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(40) Mr. Barton Antonius Michael Green, J.P.
Is recognized for over forty years of dedicated service in business development and community resilience. As leader of the St. Michael South Central District Emergency Organisation for 25 years, he has strengthened disaster preparedness and response. His leadership, commitment, and service especially during crises, reflect an enduring devotion to community welfare and national development.

(41) Mr. Christopher Wayne Griffith
Is honoured for his outstanding service in community policing and youth engagement in St. Michael. A founder of the Saving Our Community Children initiative and a champion of road tennis, he has inspired countless young people through mentorship, sport, and leadership, fostering unity, discipline, and pride within the communities he so faithfully serves.

(42) Ms. Janice Dolores Griffith
Is honoured for her unwavering dedication to community service, youth mentorship, and care for the elderly. Through her tireless work in her church and neighbourhood, she exemplifies compassion, humility, and leadership. Her consistent, selfless service and positive influence have strengthened community bonds. She continues to be a dependable role model and community leader.

(43) Mr. Anthony Carlisle O’Neil Hall, J.P.
Anthony “Paddie” Hall is awarded for his lifelong dedication to sports and community development. From his youth, he used his passion for cricket to inspire, mentor, and unite young people, fostering discipline, teamwork, and pride. His selfless service and leadership continue to cultivate a culture of pride, discipline and togetherness.

(44) Mrs. Hazeain Maria Harding-King
Mrs. Hazeain Harding-King is awarded for over 30 years of transformative service in education, literacy, and community development. As Founder and Principal of CMI Preparatory School, she has empowered children of all abilities to thrive, championed adult literacy, and mentored at-risk youth exemplifying compassion, vision, and lifelong dedication to uplifting the people of St. Michael and Barbados.

(45) Mrs. Kathleen Blossom Harper-Hall
For over fifty years of distinguished service to sport and community development, including leadership in athletics, netball, and boxing, and mentorship of generations of young people. Mrs. Harper-Hall is recognized as a trailblazer in sports administration and education and for her lifelong commitment to excellence, inclusion, and empowerment.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(46) Ms. Kathy Bernadette Harris, G.T.E., J.P.
She has enriched the lives of children, families, and the elderly through years of advocacy, volunteerism, mentorship, organizing activities, tutoring, supporting the underprivileged, and promoting wellness. Her generosity and commitment to creating inclusive, supportive spaces embody the highest ideals of community spirit.

(47) Mr. Jeffrey Anthony Headley, J.P.
A retired Director of the Environmental Protection Department, he has been a community-driven leader, particularly focused on youth engagement, environmental safety, and international advocacy. He is recognized as a leader in environmental management and education, who has championed sustainability while mentoring youth in his community. Revered as “Teacher,” Mr. Headley exemplifies service, integrity, and dedication to national and community development.

(48) Mrs. Riegina Hinds-Adams, J.P.
Is recognized for her exceptional dedication to youth development and empowerment. Through mentorship, community programs, and personal guidance, she has helped young people build confidence, develop life skills, and pursue meaningful goals. Her commitment, leadership, and selfless service have positively shaped the lives of many.

(49) Rev. David Nathaniel Holder, B.S.S.
He is a fixture of Brittons Hill. He is honoured for over thirty years of dedicated spiritual and community leadership. As Pastor of Collymore Rock Church of the Nazarene since 1991, he has nurtured faith, built strong community relationships and championed outreach programs for the youth and the elderly. His offers counsel and support to local residents, embodying Christian love and true evangelism.

(50) Mr. Errol Dacosta Holder
Mr. Errol “Scoopy” Holder is recognized for his leadership and legacy of cricket and youth development in St. Michael. As a player, coach, and mentor, he instilled discipline, inspired teamwork, and influenced resilience among young cricketers. Through tournaments, coaching, and community engagement, he strengthened the sport and community and fostered talent both on and off the field.

(51) Mrs. Sophia Harriette Holder, J.P.
Ms. Holder is awarded for decades of philanthropy and volunteerism. From back-to-school initiatives to children’s breakfast programs to support for the elderly. Her reliability, outstanding contributions and dedication to community well-being have empowered vulnerable populations and strengthened community bonds.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(52) Mr. Stefan Enrico Holder
Mr. Holder has made a lasting impact on cricket in his community and Barbados. He is awarded for his outstanding contributions to cricket, youth and community development. As a skilled player, mentor, and promoter of the sport, he has inspired young athletes, fostered teamwork, and strengthened community bonds.

(53) Mrs. Linda Cecilia Jones
Ms. Jones is recognised for her unswerving commitment to education and community development. As a teacher at Eden Lodge Primary School, mentor, leader, and through her commitment to academic and extracurricular enrichment, she has trained and empowered her students to be disciplined, pursue excellence, and exude confidence.

(54) Mr. Junior Lionel Jordan
Mr. Jordan is recognized for his advocacy and sterling contribution of over forty years to road safety and driver education in Barbados and the wider Caribbean. As President of the Barbados Road Safety Association, Board member of the Transport Authority, and founder of the Caribbean Academy of Driving Excellence, he has trained countless drivers in his community and beyond. He has also promoted professional driving standards, safe driving habits, and contributed to the well-being of his community.

(55) Ms. Ronelle Hazeain Khadija King
As founder and Executive Director of Life in Leggings, Ms. King has made significant contributions to gender equality, youth empowerment, and social justice. Through transformative initiatives such as Pink Parliament and Redefining Masculinities, she has championed marginalized voices in her community and advanced women’s leadership. She is recognised for her advocacy and humanitarian service and the protection of vulnerable groups.

(56) Mrs. Thelma Elaine Knight, J.P.
Mrs. Knight. a well-respected community leader, is honoured for her lifelong community service, philanthropy, volunteerism, and steadfast commitment to others. For many years she has made invaluable contributions to the people of St. Michael by selflessly supporting her neighbours, giving of her time and resources, leading community initiatives, and bringing joy through her generosity and kindness.

(57) Mr. Abdul Kothdiwala
As a business leader, and faith-based mentor, Mr. Kothdiwala is recognised for his outstanding contributions to sport, enterprise, and community development in St. Michael. He is the inaugural captain of the local Indian cricket team. He has pioneered innovations in the game through his leadership at the Kensington New Road Mosque. In addition, his entrepreneurial ventures improved the socioeconomic conditions of families and empowered his community at Chapman Lane.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(58) Mr. Mark Anthony Lorde
Mr. Lorde is a cherished performer, mentor, and cultural ambassador. He is being honoured for sixty years of outstanding contribution to preserving Barbados’ musical heritage, enriching its cultural landscape and uplifting his community through his artistry. From his home in Bayville, he has trained and nurtured the talent of young people in finding their voice. His iconic anthem “My Country to Me” and lifelong devotion to youth and cultural development, embody his unmatched contribution to Barbadian music and his devotion to his community.

(59) Mrs. Margaret Ezralyne Toni Marshall
Mrs. Marshall is being honoured for her sterling contributions to public service, social justice and human dignity. She is acknowledged for her achievements and selfless service as an educator, social worker, community advocate, and church leader who has left an indelible mark and made a difference whilst advocating for the protection of children, the welfare of vulnerable families, and the dignity of the elderly.

(60) Mr. Robert Ziggy Marshall, J.P.
Mr. Robert Ziggy Marshall is a humble, compassionate, consistent leader, and peacemaker who has demonstrated exemplary leadership, civic responsibility and outstanding service to community development, youth empowerment, and disaster preparedness. He is commended for his volunteerism, mentorship, mediation and unstinting commitment to improving socio-economic conditions and building community resilience.

(61) Mr. Renaldo Athelston Maughan
Mr. Renaldo Maughn is synonymous with basketball in the Pine. He has devoted over fifty years to developing basketball and young people in the Pinelands community. As a visionary coach, mentor, and leader, he is honoured for transforming the Princess Royal court into a hub and powerhouse of national basketball excellence, which has produced national players and champions. His tireless dedication to the sport, and to his community is to be commended.

(62) Mr. Michael Anderson Mayers
Mr. Mayers is recognized for more than twenty years of dedicated service to community empowerment, enterprise development, youth mentorship, and civic engagement. Through his leadership of initiatives at the Lime Bar, renovations to the Bush Hall Community Centre, mentoring, and skills training for young people, he has strengthened social ties, revitalized community spaces, enhanced the well-being of his community and facilitated economic opportunity within the parish of St. Michael.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(63) Mr. David St. Elmo Miller
Mr. Miller is a dedicated community organizer, respected leader, philanthropist and stalwart of Brittons Hill, St. Michael who quietly supports vulnerable families, empowers youth and promotes community cohesion through sporting and social initiatives. As a core member of the National Peace Programme football tournament, he has used football as a powerful tool to mentor young people, foster discipline, inspire resilience and unite the community.

(64) Mr. Vincent Miller
Born and raised at Leinster Road, St. Michael, Mr. Miller is awarded for his volunteerism, selfless community service and dedication to the welfare of his neighbourhood. A skilled carpenter and tailor, he walked through his neighbourhood proactively securing homes, safeguarding families before severe weather, and selflessly repaired damaged homes afterwards without expecting compensation. His unwavering dedication, generosity, and hands-on support is a shining example of true community spirit.

(65) Ms. Elizabeth Gina Millington
Ms. Elizabeth “Aunty Gina” Millington is honoured for over forty years of significant service and outstanding achievements in the Black Rock and Deacons Farm communities. She is the founder of the Deacons Farm Action Group and Deacons Cultural Group. She mentors young people as a Blossom and Brownie Guider, and transforms lives through cultural and educational initiatives, leading community development projects, and contributing significantly to the YWCA and the Parish Independence Committee.

(66) Mr. Samuel Galwyn Murray
Mr. Samuel Murray stands as a true giant within the football-rich Pinelands community. He has dedicated his time and efforts to developing football talent in Pinelands, excelling as both a player and a coach. From leading junior teams to Under-18 championships, to guiding Pinelands to the Premier League, his mentorship, vision, and commitment have shaped generations of athletes. He is being honoured for his enduring legacy and impact on youth, sport, and community development.

(67) Mrs. Gail Michelle Peters, J.P.
A lifelong Bayville resident, Mrs. Peters is recognised for her distinguished record of community service, youth mentorship, outreach, and care of the elderly. As President of Bayville Women in Action and a Justice of the Peace, she has improved the lives of residents and women in particular through initiatives including cleanups, sports, Back-to-School drives, and holiday support. Her committed leadership and compassion are aimed at improving the lives of others.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(68) Ms. Clare Lena Natasha Phillips
Ms. Clare Phillips is awarded for her sterling achievements in mentorship, care of the elderly, and community service in her parish. From guiding young people, supporting seniors, and assisting families, to leading food drives and disaster response initiatives, her compassion, leadership, and tireless dedication have transformed lives, uplifted vulnerable populations and strengthened community resilience.

(69) Ms. Yvonne Patricia Phillips
Ms. Yvonne Philips is a positive role model who exemplifies extraordinary resilience, and selfless service. Despite losing both legs, she has overcome personal adversity to render steadfast support to her community. For this she is honoured and recognised for volunteering at events, preparing meals, and supporting neighbors. Her strength and courage are an inspiration and embody the highest standards of civic responsibility.

(70) Mr. Christopher Macdonald Reece
Mr. Christopher Reece is acknowledged for his exceptional leadership, impactful mentorship, and unswerving dedication to inspiring civic pride. He has consistently dedicated his time, energy, and expertise to initiatives that encouraged active participation in community life. He has provided guidance, support, and encouragement to young people facing challenges, helping them navigate obstacles and in making positive choices to reach their potential.

(71) Mr. Darnley Alfonso Reece
Mr. Darnley Reece is honoured for thirty-five years of dedicated service to St. Michael and to the Barbados Citizen Band Radio Association. He has shown steadfast commitment to ensuring vital emergency communications are disseminated, providing reassurance and stability during times of national need, and supporting community initiatives. His unwavering devotion, community support, and enduring contributions to the safety and well-being of others are deserving of recognition.

(72) Ms. Marcia Thelmina Reece
Ms. Reece is honoured for forty years of exceptional service as an educator at the Eden Lodge Primary School and for her transformative impact on her community. Not only ensuring that each child under her care received a quality education but also guiding and encouraging young people to embrace their self- worth and maximise their potential. She is leaving a lasting legacy of academic excellence and community enrichment.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(73) Mr. Shamar Pierre Reece
Mr. Shamar Reece is a committed community leader whose initiatives have enriched the City of Bridgetown and beyond. He is honoured for his outstanding service and leadership of beautification projects, youth development workshops, job recruitment drives, and charitable sporting events that have created opportunities and uplifted underserved families. His dedication to back-to-school campaigns and Christmas give-back initiatives exemplifies his unwavering commitment to service and community empowerment.

(74) Mr. Fabian Ricardo Reeves
Founder and President of the Black Knights Bikers Club, Mr. Reeves is recognised for his transformative leadership, anti-bullying programs, support for charitable initiatives, road safety advocacy, and humanitarian service. He is honoured for empowering youth, supporting families in need, and redefining community engagement through mentorship, philanthropy, and civic responsibility.

(75) Ms. Eleanor Idelia Rice, J.P.
Community Service Officer, radio host, cultural leader, and arts advocate. Ms. Rice is honoured for her outstanding achievements in community rehabilitation, mental health awareness, broadcasting, mentorship, and the performing arts. Through her exceptional leadership and creativity, she has improved people’s social and emotional wellbeing, inspired underserved communities, and enriched Barbados’ cultural landscape for over thirty years.

(76) Mr. Listial Alexander Boyce
For his unwavering dedication to the Grazettes and Wavell Avenue communities, Mr. Boyce demonstrates exceptional leadership and philanthropy. Through mentoring youth, providing school supplies, supporting local organisations, and offering training and employment opportunities, he has strengthened community bonds and positively impacted the lives of those in need.

(77) Ms. Yvette Arnella Maxine Cox
Ms. Cox is recognised for her outstanding dedication to the St. Stephen’s Hill community in St. Michael. Through mentorship, selfless care for the elderly, and guidance of children and youth, she has contributed to their spiritual grounding and wellbeing, whilst demonstrating exceptional leadership, compassion, and service.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(78) Ms. Ann Roseta Harewood, J.P.
Ms. Harewood is honoured as a resolute community leader who has given outstanding and selfless service to Wavell Avenue and the wider Black Rock communities. Deeply committed to the wellbeing of others, she has devoted her life to caring for children, the elderly, and the vulnerable. Ms. Harewood is known for her compassion, philanthropy and generosity of spirit.

(79) Ms. Yvette Nicole Hunte
An accomplished educator and community leader with fifteen years of distinguished service in education and administration, Ms. Hunte has guided and supported children through programs at the Eden Lodge Primary School and Empire Sports Camp. She is being honoured for her exemplary leadership, mentorship, volunteerism, and significant contributions to youth development and community empowerment.

(80) Ms. Angela Dorcey Pauline Inniss, J.P.
Ms. Inniss is lauded as an educator philanthropist, farmer, community leader and stalwart from St. Michael. She has devoted over thirty years to ensuring the wellbeing of young children through St. Ann’s Kindergarten. Guided by her Christian faith, she selflessly supports needy families, fostering their education and wholistic development.

(81) Ms. Julene Marketta Kellman
An educator and community advocate, Ms. Kellman is honoured for thirty years of significant contributions to the advancement of the vulnerable people in the parish of St. Michael. Nurturing young minds as a caring and committed teacher and mentor, and through her volunteer tutoring and service with the Olive Branch of Hope Foundation. In addition, she has supported children and families affected by cancer.

(82) Mr. Shawn Roger Lingwood Ruck, J.P.
Mr. Ruck is recognised for his outstanding leadership, pastoral care and community service in the Brittons Hill community. Through the Shepney Construction, school, his ministry, and mentorship, he has mobilized resources, offered refuge, provided training for young people and artisans in modern building practices, and afforded opportunities for all, especially those in need.

(83) Mr. Dale Randolph Rudder
A celebrated soca artiste, cultural ambassador, community leader and sports advocate, Mr. Dale “Mistah Dale” Rudder is awarded for his exceptional contributions to the advancement of Barbadian culture, youth, and community development. Through his civic service, specialised programmes, music and mentorship he has strengthened our cultural identity, inspired creativity, instilled discipline, and fostered social cohesion within the Deacons Farm and other St. Michael communities.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(84) Ms. Latoya Shondelle Scott
Ms. Scott, a proud daughter of St. Michael, has rendered exceptional community service through her entrepreneurship and philanthropy. She is honoured for selflessly dedicating her home, time, and resources to caring for the elderly and supporting children in Spooner’s Hill, St. Michael by providing hot meals, afterschool
care, and mentorship.

(85) Mr. Ian Charles Small
For his pioneering contribution to sporting and community life. As a gifted player, coach, and mentor, Mr. Small is recognised for transforming the sport of basketball into a force for community building and youth empowerment. His leadership, rare blend of discipline and passion have inspired and shaped the character and talent of young men from Dayrell’s Road and Paddock Road to take the national stage, earning him enduring respect as a true icon of St.
Michael.

(86) Ms. Shelly Rosita Small
At the heart of the Pinelands community stands Ms. Shelly Small. She is honoured for her significant contributions as a cultural ambassador who has profoundly impacted Barbados’ heritage through dance education and African Awareness initiatives. Her leadership and sterling efforts have inspired artistic self-expression among young people, influenced them to embrace their cultural identity whilst highlighting community pride and excellence.

(87) Mr. Dean Armand Squires
Mr. Squires is recognised for his exceptional dedication to youth empowerment through sport and faith. Using the vehicle of Combined Faith Sports Ministry, he twinned his passion for basketball and his faith, to transform the lives of at- risk youth through mentorship, technical training and life skills. He is commended for his tireless service, volunteerism and faith-based leadership.

(88) Mr. Marcus Sylvester Stephen, J.P.
Mr. Stephen is awarded for rendering over forty years of outstanding yeoman service to youth and community development. Through sports, mentorship, and leading national outreach efforts as Coordinator of the Block Transformation Unit, he championed the empowerment of at-risk youth, created viable employment opportunities for underserved young people, and provided charitable support for vulnerable families.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(89) Ms. Erma Ione Thornhill
A distinguished award-winning senior athlete, Ms. Thornhill, is recognised for her outstanding athletic achievements and advocacy for healthy ageing. Through her leadership in the Barbados Masters and Seniors Athletic Club, this avid supporter of senior health programs, and multiple gold medalist at the 2024 Pennsylvania Senior Games, continues to be a role model in her community promoting fitness, wellness, and active living among Barbadian seniors.

(90) Mr. Kevin Andre Watson
Mr. Watson, known as “Sluggy Dan”, has dedicated twenty years to “paying it forward” and providing at-risk youth, as he was, with the necessary tools to aspire to a brighter future and to transform their lives. He is awarded for his impactful advocacy and dedication to youth empowerment. Through music, mentorship, and humanitarian outreach, he has guided hundreds of marginalised young people toward positive purpose and life-changing opportunities.

(91) Mr. Hal Anthony Chesterfield Welch
For thirty years of outstanding community service, Mr. Hal Welch is recognised for his leadership and sterling contributions to uplifting communities through faith, mentorship, and practical outreach. As a pastor, counselor, and martial arts instructor, he has empowered youth, supported families, and fostered community resilience and hope, through practical outreach and Christian values across Bayville, Bayland, and Brittons Hill.

(92) Mr. Anthony Leroy Williams
Mr. Anthony “Big Mark” Williams is recognized for his unwavering dedication to the care of elderly persons, persons with disabilities, and for his selfless assistance to vulnerable residents in the Haggatt Hall and Dash Valley communities. Despite personal physical challenges, he provides transportation, hampers, and daily assistance, maintaining the well-being of those in need.

(93) Mrs. Nadera Deandrea Williams
Mrs. Nadera Williams has demonstrated leadership, compassion, and reliability beyond her years. Whether organising cleanups, supporting youth programs, or assisting families in need, she consistently uplifts her community and inspires others to serve. She is honoured for her exceptional commitment to community service and volunteerism.

(94) Mr. Robert DeCosta Williams
Mr. Robert Williams has devoted over thirty years to the Barbados Citizen Band Radio Association and to community service in St. Michael. Renowned for his reliability and teamwork, he is awarded for his significant contributions to emergency operations and preparedness, community mentorship, and strengthening social cohesion.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(95) Ms. Calisa Shontai Azalea Wilson
Ms. Calisa Wilson, an aspiring educator from Chapman Lane, is awarded for her significant achievements in education and community development, leading the Learning in Harmony Homework Programme and enhancing literacy and numeracy since 2021. In addition, she is being recognised for her passionate advocacy for early childhood development, and steadfast commitment to inspiring children and youth through innovative teaching.

(96) Mr. Philip Anthony Wilson
For a lifetime of distinguished service, Mr. Philip Anthony Wilson is recognised for his sterling contributions to his parish through entrepreneurship, professional excellence, leadership, and community mentorship. As an accountant, business leader, lecturer, and volunteer, he has shared knowledge, guided youth, and supported social causes in St. Michael and beyond. His integrity, dedication, and civic commitment are commendable.

(97) Ms. Juliet Worrell
Ms. Worrell is honoured for her steadfast dedication to promoting and preserving Barbados’ indigenous sport, Road Tennis. Through mentorship, event organisation, coaching and grassroots outreach, she has fostered community pride and participation in the sport. As a committed member of the Barbados Road Tennis Association, she has also inspired young people to play the sport and ensured the sport’s accessibility to everyone.

(98) Ms. Margarita Elizabeth Yarde
Ms. Yarde is being recognised for her significant contributions to national communications and public safety through the Barbados Citizen Band Radio Association, and her unwavering commitment to improving community life and supporting local and national mass crowd events. Her volunteerism, reliability, leadership, organizational skills, and mentorship have strengthened community readiness and engagement.

(99) Mr. Dahrean Antonio Mario Yearwood
Mr. Dahrean Yearwood is recognised for twenty years of volunteerism and dedicated community service in his parish. He has made significant contributions to youth empowerment, community outreach, resource mobilisation, disaster preparedness and public safety. His leadership of various initiatives improved living conditions and created opportunities for many, particularly young people and assisted in building more sustainable communities.

WE GATHERIN’ 2025 HONOURS LIST – ST. MICHAEL – (Cont’d)

(100) Mr. Edwin Patrick Yearwood
With his roots remaining firmly planted in Bayville, St. Michael, this acclaimed performing artiste, songwriter, and cultural ambassador, inspires and nurtures young musical ability, supports schools’ initiatives, participates in community events, keeps the peace and showcases Barbadian talent locally and internationally. Mr. Edwin “The General” Yearwood is honoured for his impeccable artistry, steadfast commitment to volunteerism and philanthropy, and exceptional contributions to highlighting Barbados’ cultural heritage and strengthening the pride of his home community.

NAMES OF PERSONS INTENDED TO BE DELETED FROM THE REGISTER OF ELECTORS
published on or before January 31, 2026, considered as being Deceased.

FIRST PUBLIC NOTICE

(Section 9(2) of Representation of the People Act. Cap.12)

ELECTORAL AND BOUNDARIES COMMISSION

The Electoral and Boundaries Commission hereby gives notice that:

  1. Pursuant to Section 9 of the Representation of the People Act Cap.12 of the Laws of Barbados, it intends to consider the deletion of names of persons from the Register of Electors published on or before January 31, 2026 under Section 13 of the said Act.

The names of the persons to be deleted may be viewed on the website of the Electoral and Boundaries Commission at www.ebc.gov.bb and at the office of the Electoral and Boundaries Commission. The names shall also be published in the national print media.

By way of this Notice, the Electoral and Boundaries Commission is requesting anyone having information in respect of whether any person whose name appears on the list is NOT dead or overseas for 5 years or more, to submit such information to the Office at Level 1, Warrens Towers II, Warrens, St. Michael or via email at electoral@barbados.gov.bb, no later than Sunday, December 21, 2025.

Ramon Alleyne, S.C. Chairman
Electoral and Boundaries Commission 2025-11-22

NAMES OF PERSONS INTENDED TO BE DELETED FROM THE REGISTER OF ELECTORS

FIRST PUBLIC NOTICE

ELECTORAL AND BOUNDARIES COMMISSION

The Electoral and Boundaries Commission hereby gives notice that:

  1. Pursuant to Section 9 of the Representation of the People Act Cap.12 of the Laws of Barbados, it intends to consider the deletion of names of persons from the Register of Electors published on or before January 31, 2026 under Section 13 of the said Act.

The names of the persons to be deleted may be viewed on the website of the Electoral and Boundaries Commission at www.ebc.gov.bb and at the office of the Electoral and Boundaries Commission. The names shall also be published in the national print media.

By way of this Notice, the Electoral and Boundaries Commission is requesting anyone having information in respect of whether any person whose name appears on the list is NOT dead or overseas for 5 years or more, to submit such information to the Office at Level 1, Warrens Towers II, Warrens, St. Michael or via email at electoral@barbados.gov.bb, no later than Sunday, December 21, 2025.

COMPANIES (ECONOMIC SUBSTANCE) (REPEAL) ACT, 2025

OBJECTS AND REASONS

This  Bill  would  repeal  the  Companies  (Economic  Substance)  Act,  2019

(Act 2019-43) and provide for related matters.

COMPANIES (ECONOMIC SUBSTANCE) (REPEAL) ACT, 2025

Arrangement of Sections

  1. Short title
  • Repeal of Act 2019-43
  • Transitional
  • Commencement

BARBADOS

A Bill entitled

An  Act  to  repeal  the  Companies  (Economic  Substance)  Act,       2019

(Act 2019-43).

ENACTED by the Parliament of Barbados as follows:

Short title

1.

This  Act  may  be  cited  as  the  Companies  (Economic Substance)

(Repeal) Act, 2025.

Repeal of Act 2019-43

2.

repealed.

The Companies (Economic Substance) Act, 2019 (Act 2019-43) is

Transitional

3.(1)

(a)

Notwithstanding section 2, all

  • rights, powers, privileges and functions relating to the administration and enforcement of the former Act shall continue to be exercisable;
    • rights, obligations and liabilities of a company under the former Act and subsisting immediately before the commencement of this Act shall continue to subsist;
    • remedies available under the former Act shall continue to be available; and
    • proceedings commenced under the former Act may be continued,

in respect of any fiscal period ending on or before the 31st day of December, 2024, as if the former Act had not been repealed; and

(b) any Guidelines issued under the former Act shall, for the purposes of paragraph (a), continue to apply in respect of a fiscal period ending on or before the 31st day of December, 2024, as if the former Act had not been repealed.

  • For the avoidance of doubt, in relation to any fiscal period ending in 2025

and for every subsequent fiscal period, the Income Tax Act, Cap. 73 shall apply in relation to any requirement for a company to have economic substance.

  • In this section,

“economic substance” has the meaning assigned to it by section 52F of the Income Tax Act, Cap. 73;

“fiscal period” has the meaning assigned to it by section 85 of the Income Tax Act, Cap. 73;

“former   Act”   means   the   Companies   (Economic   Substance)   Act,   2019

(Act 2019-43).

Commencement

4.

2025.

This Act is deemed to have come into operation the 1st day of January,

INCOME TAX (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2025

OBJECTS AND REASONS

This Bill would amend the Income Tax Act, Cap. 73 to impose economic substance requirements that are consistent with international standards on companies benefiting from preferential tax regimes, and provide for related matters.

INCOME TAX (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2025

Arrangement of Sections

  1. Short title
  • Insertion of new Division into Cap. 73
  • Commencement

BARBADOS

A Bill entitled

An Act to amend the Income Tax Act, Cap. 73. ENACTED by the Parliament of Barbados as follows:

Short title 1.

This Act may be cited as the Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 2025.

Insertion of new Division into Cap. 73

2.                        The Income Tax Act, Cap. 73 is amended by inserting after Division

V, the following:

“DIVISION VA

Economic Substance Compliance and Reporting

Application of Division VA

52A.(1)

This Division applies in respect of income year 2025    and

every subsequent income year.

  • Sections 52B, 52C and 52D apply to a company that
    • derives income from carrying on a relevant activity in an income year; and
    • is liable to tax at a rate of less than 9 per cent under section 43A(3A) or 43(9)(b).
    • Section 52E applies to a company that is liable to tax at a rate

of less than 9 per cent under section 43B.

Economic substance requirements

52B.(1)

substance.

A company described in section 52A(2) shall have economic

  • Subject to subsection (6), the company shall, for the purposes

of subsection (1),

  • conduct its core income-generating activities in Barbados; and
    • comply with the requirements set out in subsection (3),

in relation to a relevant activity carried on in Barbados in an income year.

  • The requirements referred to in subsection (2)(b) are that the

company

(a)

(b)

is directed and managed in Barbados, and its decision- making processes are carried out in Barbados; and

has, having regard to the nature and level of income derived from the relevant activity,

  • an adequate amount of operating expenditure incurred in Barbados, which is proportionate to the level of activity carried on in Barbados;
  • an adequate physical presence in Barbados, including maintaining a place of business, an office, premises or plant, property and equipment for the purpose of carrying on the activity; and
  • an adequate number of employees or other personnel, with appropriate qualifications, who are physically present in Barbados.
  • A company may outsource to another person in Barbados its

core income-generating activities in relation to a relevant activity carried on in Barbados, if the company is able to monitor and control the conduct of the core income-generating activity by the other person.

  • A company is directed and managed in Barbados if
    • the board of directors of the company meets in Barbados at an adequate frequency, given the level of decision-making required;
    • during each meeting of the board of directors, there is a quorum of directors physically present at the meeting in Barbados;
  • strategic decisions of the company are made at meetings of the board of directors, and minutes of the meetings reflect the decisions;
    • the board of directors, as a whole, have the necessary knowledge and expertise to discharge its duties as a board; and
    • the minutes of all board meetings and the records of the company are kept in Barbados.
  • A company is not required to comply with subsections (1), (2)

and (3) in an income year if it has no gross income in relation to the relevant activity carried on in the income year.

Economic substance reporting

52C.(1)

A company shall, in respect of income year 2025 and    for

every subsequent income year, include in its return filed pursuant to section 52 such information as the Commissioner may require for the Commissioner to determine whether the company complies with section 52B.

(2)       The information referred to in subsection (1) shall be provided

in the manner and form prescribed by the Commissioner.

Economic substance compliance audit etc.

52D.(1)

The Commissioner may conduct an audit of a company  to

determine whether the company complies with section 52B.

  • An audit may include
    • a review of the financial records of the company, including accounting documents, invoices and contracts, in order to assess the adequacy of operating expenditure incurred in Barbados;
  • a verification of the physical presence of the company in Barbados, including the location and nature of its premises, plant, property, and equipment;
    • an examination of the employment records and contracts of the company in order to assess the number, qualifications and roles of employees or other personnel present in Barbados;
    • a review of the governance and decision-making processes of the company to ensure that it is directed and managed in Barbados; and
    • any other investigation relevant to determining whether the company has complied with section 52B.
  • Subsections (1) and (2) are without prejudice to any duties or

powers imposed or conferred under section 76 in relation to the administration and enforcement of this Act, including the power to request additional information.

  • Where, after an audit under this section or an assessment under

section 53, the Commissioner determines that a company has not complied with section 52B in respect of an income year

  • section 43(9)(b) or 43A(3A), as the case may be, shall not apply to the company; and
    • the Commissioner shall make an assessment or re- assessment, as the case may be, of the amount of tax payable for the income year by the company at the rate specified in section 43(8).
  • Where the Commissioner assesses or re-assesses the amount of

tax payable for an income year by a company as a result of its failure to comply with section 52B, the Commissioner shall deliver a notice of

assessment or notice of re-assessment to the company, as the case may be, setting out

  • the basis on which the assessment or re-assessment was made;
    • the amount of tax payable as a result of the assessment or re- assessment; and
    • the period within which the tax must be paid.
  • The provisions of this Act relating to objections under section

57 and appeals under sections 58 to 63 apply, with the necessary modifications and adaptations, in relation to an assessment or reassessment made under this section.

Companies taxed under section 43B

52E.

For the avoidance of doubt, a company that is liable to  tax

under section 43B shall be regarded as having economic substance.

Interpretation of Division VA

52F.

In this Division,

“core income-generating activities” means activities required for a company to generate income in relation to a relevant activity, and includes in respect of

  • insurance business,
    • predicting or calculating risk or oversight of the prediction or calculation of risk;
    • insuring or re-insuring against risk; and
    • providing insurance business services to clients;
  • international shipping business
    • managing    crew,    including    hiring,    paying   and overseeing crew members;
    • overhauling and maintaining ships;
    • overseeing and tracking deliveries;
    • determining what goods to order and when to deliver them; and
    • organising and overseeing voyages;

“economic substance”, in relation to a company, means a real and substantial economic presence in Barbados;

“relevant activity” means insurance business or international shipping business.”.

Commencement

3.                        This Act is deemed to have come into operation on the 1st day of

January, 2025.

Read three times and passed the House of Assembly this day of        , 2025.

Speaker

Read three times and passed the Senate this               day of

, 2025.

President

CONSTITUTION (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2025

OBJECTS AND REASONS

This Bill would amend the Constitution to

  • provide for the election of a person who is not a member of either House to the office of Speaker of the House of Assembly; and
    • enable a Minister to address the House of which he is not a member on any matter within his portfolio and the Attorney-General to address either House on any matter.

CONSTITUTION (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2025

Arrangement of Sections

  1. Short title
  • Insertion of sections 45A, 45B and 45C into the Constitution
  • Insertion of section 53A into the Constitution
  • Amendment of the Third Schedule

BARBADOS

A Bill entitled

An Act to amend the Constitution.

ENACTED by the Parliament of Barbados in accordance with the provisions of section 49 of the Constitution as follows:

Short title 1.

This Act may be cited as the Constitution (Amendment) Act, 2025.

Insertion of sections 45A, 45B and 45C into the Constitution

2.

following:

The  Constitution  is  amended  by  inserting  after  section  45  the

“Speaker and Deputy Speaker

45A.(1)

There shall be a Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House

of Assembly who shall be elected in accordance with the provisions of this section.

  • When the House of Assembly first meets after any dissolution

of Parliament and before it proceeds to the despatch of any other business, it shall elect a person who is not a member of the House of Assembly or the Senate to be the Speaker; and whenever the office of Speaker becomes vacant for any reason other than a dissolution of Parliament, the House shall, as soon as practicable, elect another such person to that office.

  • The Speaker shall, by virtue of holding the office of Speaker,

be deemed to be a member of the House of Assembly in addition to the thirty members or such greater number of members as may be prescribed by Parliament pursuant to section 41(1).

  • The Speaker shall, whenever on a division the votes are equal,

have a casting vote.

  • When the House of Assembly first meets after any dissolution

of Parliament and before it proceeds to the despatch of any other business, except the election of the Speaker, the House shall elect a member of the House who is not a Minister or Parliamentary Secretary to be Deputy Speaker, and if the office of Deputy Speaker becomes vacant for any reason other than a dissolution of Parliament, the House shall, as soon as practicable, elect another such person to that office.

  • A person shall not be elected Speaker or Deputy Speaker if
    • he is not a citizen of Barbados; or
    • he is a person disqualified for election as a member of the House of Assembly by virtue of section 44(1) or any other law enacted pursuant to section 44(2).
  • The Speaker shall be entitled to such conditions of service as

may be prescribed by Parliament.

Vacation of office by Speaker and Deputy Speaker

45B.(1)

(a)

A person shall vacate the office of Speaker

  • when the House first meets after any dissolution of Parliament;
  • where he ceases to be a citizen of Barbados;
  • any circumstances arise that would cause him to be disqualified for election as a member of the House by virtue of section 44(1) or any law enacted pursuant to section 44(2); or
  • where he announces the resignation of his office to the House of Assembly or, if by writing under his hand addressed to the Clerk of the House, he resigns that office; and

(b) Deputy Speaker where he announces the resignation of his office to the House of Assembly or if by writing under his hand addressed, to the Speaker or, if the office of Speaker is vacant or the Speaker is absent from Barbados, to the Clerk of the House, he resigns that office.

(2)       A Speaker shall no longer be deemed to be a member of the

House of Assembly pursuant to section 45A(3) if he has vacated the office of Speaker.

Removal of Speaker and Deputy Speaker

45C.(1)

Standing Orders made pursuant to section 50 may  provide

for the removal of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker from office.

  • A Speaker shall no longer be deemed to be a member of the

House pursuant to section 45A(3) if he is removed from the office of Speaker.”.

Insertion of section 53A into the Constitution

3.

following:

The  Constitution  is  amended  by  inserting  after  section  53  the

“Attendance of Ministers in either House

53A.(1)

A Minister who is a Member of the House of Assembly and

a Minister who is a Senator

  • may attend any sitting of the Senate or the House of Assembly, respectively; and
    • may be required at the instance of the President of the Senate or the Speaker to attend any sitting of the Senate or the House of Assembly, respectively.
  • A Minister may not be required to attend any sitting of either

House under subsection (1)(b) except on the adoption by that House of a motion for the purpose.

  • A Minister attending any sitting of the Senate or the House of

Assembly under subsection (1) may take part in any debate or other

proceedings concerning matters falling within his portfolio in such House and may speak only on any motion before the House concerning his portfolio and move amendments to any such motions, save that such a Minister shall have no vote thereon.

  • Nothing in this section shall preclude the Attorney-General

from attending any sitting of the Senate or the House of Assembly, as the case may be, and taking part in debates and other proceedings and speaking on any motion before any such House, as the case may be, and moving amendments to any such motions even though the matter falls within the portfolio of some other Minister.”.

Amendment of the Third Schedule

4.              The Third Schedule to the Constitution is amended by deleting

paragraph 2 and substituting the following:

“2. The number of persons entitled to vote in any one constituency shall, so far as practicable, be not more than 120 per cent, nor less than 80 per cent, of the total number of persons entitled to vote in Barbados, divided by the total number of the constituencies.”.

BARBADOS HARBOURS (AMENDMENT) REGULATIONS, 2025
The Minister, in exercise of the powers conferred on him by section 13(2) of the Barbados Port Inc. (Transfer of Management and Vesting of Assets) Act, makes the following Regulations:

Citation

  1. These Regulations may be cited as the Barbados Harbours (Amendment) Regulations, 2025.

Amendment of regulation 2 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Paragraph (1) of regulation 2 of the Barbados Harbours Regulations, 1961 (L.N. 11 of 1961), in these Regulations referred to as the principal Regulations, is amended by deleting the definition “management” and substituting the following:
    “ “management” means the person or persons from time to time appointed to perform the duties of the Chief Executive Officer of the Port, and includes his deputies or assistants;”.

Amendment of regulation 3 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Paragraph (1) of regulation 3 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:
    S.I. 2025 No. 84
    “3.(1) The persons who may serve as berthing masters shall be those appointed by the Port Chief Executive Officer after examination as provided in this regulation.”.

Amendment of regulation 5 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. The shoulder note and paragraph (1) of regulation 5 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Exemption from compulsory pilotage
5.(1) When a ship is exempted from compulsory pilotage by the Chief Executive Officer of the Port, a certificate of exemption shall, on payment of the charge prescribed in the Tariff Book, be issued by the Chief Executive Officer of the Port to the master of the ship concerned, and unless suspended or revoked shall remain in force until the end of the year in which it is issued.”.

Repeal of regulation 7 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 7 of the principal Regulations is deleted.
  2. Regulation 15 of the principal Regulations is deleted.
  3. Regulation 21 of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal of regulation 15 of L.N. 11 of 1961
Repeal of regulation 21 of L.N. 11 of 1961

Repeal and replacement of regulation 26 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 26 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:
    S.I. 2025 No. 84

“Assignment of berths and control of berthing
26.(1) The Chief Executive Officer of the Port may determine the harbour in which a ship shall berth or anchor and to assign a berth, whether at a quay or elsewhere, to each ship and, where a berth is so assigned to a ship, the ship shall occupy that berth and shall at the direction of the Chief Executive Officer of the Port be removed to any other berth that he may direct.
(1A) A Master or person in charge of a ship shall obey the directions of the Chief Executive Officer of the Port.
(2)
The Chief Executive Officer of the Port may control the berthing and mooring arrangements of every ship accommodated at a private wharf or jetty.

(3)
Ships proceeding alongside a quay shall have no list, but shall be trimmed upright.”.

Amendment of regulation 29 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 29 of the principal Regulations is amended by deleting paragraph (1) and inserting the following:
    “29.(1) Every ship within a compulsory pilotage harbour, other than a small craft, shall have sufficient hands on board to attend to her moorings and to cause them to be slackened or hove in as may be necessary.
    (1A) No rope shall be made fast except to dolphins, mooring posts and bollards placed for the purpose, and no mooring rope shall be used unless the bollards and the edge of the coping of the wharf or jetty are protected from chafe to the satisfaction of the management.
    S.I. 2025 No. 84
    (1B) No chain cable shall be used for mooring alongside except with the permission of the management.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 30 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 30 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Lights on ships and collision regulations

  1. All ships, whether under way or at anchor, shall, except as otherwise provided by these Regulations, between the hours of sunset and sunrise, exhibit the lights required by the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972, as amended.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 32 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 32 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Liability for damage in harbours

  1. The owner of every ship shall be answerable to Barbados Port Inc. for any damage done to any harbour works, plant, machinery or other property used by or for the purposes of Barbados Port Inc. by the ship or by any person employed about it, and the master or person having charge of a ship through whose wilful act or negligence any such damage is occasioned shall also be liable to make good the same.”.
    S.I. 2025 No. 84
    Amendment of regulation 40 of L.N. 11 of 1961
  2. Regulation 40 of the principal Regulations is amended by deleting paragraph (1A) and substituting the following:
    “(1A) Notwithstanding paragraph (l) and regulation 41, the management may, if it thinks it expedient, without a written request from any party, by notice in writing given to the master or person in charge and the agents in Barbados of any ship which occupies a quay berth require such ship to take in or discharge its cargo during any time and on any day specified in the notice, subject to the weather and the availability of labour for the purpose; and, if the ship fails to comply with the notice, the ship shall lose its turn to take in or discharge its cargo and may be removed from its berth by the management at the risk and expense of the ship”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 41 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 41 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following is substituted:

“Overtime work

  1. Work ashore and afloat in connection with the landing, shipping and transhipping of goods during hours other than the regular working hours of a harbour shall be charged for as overtime, and shall only be worked on receipt of a written request from the party desiring the work performed, to whom an account for the cost thereof shall be rendered by the management.”.
    Repeal of regulation 42 of L.N. 11 of 1961
  2. Regulation 42 of the principal Regulations is repealed.
    S.I. 2025 No. 84

Repeal of regulation 43 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 43 of the principal Regulations is repealed.

Repeal of regulation 45 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 45 of the principal Regulations is repealed.

Repeal and replacement of regulations 48 and 49 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulations 48 and 49 of the principal Regulations are deleted and the following substituted:

“Fire on ships
48.(1) In the event of a fire occurring on board a ship in a harbour, the master shall at once give the alarm and take such steps towards the protection of property as the Chief Executive Officer of the Port may direct.
(2) The alarm signal for ships (other than for small craft) on fire shall be consistent with the requirements for alarm signals for ships specified in the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, as amended, and the International Code of Signals.

Insanitary conditions and nuisances
49.(1) The master of a ship lying in a harbour shall ensure that all outlets or scuppers in the ship’s sides are fitted with adequate shields to prevent all obnoxious or dirty fluid or matter from falling on to the quays.
(2) Exhaust pipes shall be equipped so as to comply with Annex VI of the International Convention for the Prevention of Marine Pollution from Ships, 1973, as modified by the Protocol of 1978 and the Protocol of 1997 relating to it.
S.I. 2025 No. 84
(3) No ship shall make thick smoke or unnecessary noise that is inconsistent with the requirements for alarm signals for ships as specified in the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, as amended, and the International Code of Signals.”.

Repeal of regulations 50 and 51 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulations 50 and 51 of the principal Regulations are deleted.

Repeal of regulation 53 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 53 of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal and replacement of regulations 54 to 56 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulations 54 to 56 of the principal Regulations are deleted and the following substituted:

“No timber allowed to float in a harbour
54.(1) No timber shall be permitted to float in a harbour unless permission in writing for that purpose has been obtained from the management, and then only
(a)
in accordance with the Code of Safe Practice for Ships Carrying Timber Deck Cargoes; and

(b)
on payment of rent at the same rate as if it had been landed.

(2) The consignee of timber shall be responsible for any damage caused by the timber and any loss or customs duties, rates, charges and other losses that may result from loss of the timber.

Removal of ships with dangerous matter on board

  1. The management may order the removal from a harbour of any ship that has on board dangerous, hazardous and poisonous goods
    S.I. 2025 No. 84
    or other matter that in the opinion of the management are injurious to health, and such goods or matter shall be disposed of in such manner as it may direct at the risk and expense of the ship.

Dangerous goods
56.(1) The management may, with the consent of the Comptroller of Customs, and after giving at least 2 hours’ notice to the owner or consignee entitled to receive the goods, if the owner or consignee can be found, order the removal and, if necessary, the destruction of any goods or matter that in the opinion of the management are dangerous, hazardous and poisonous goods and that may be landed or placed upon the wharves, jetties or quays, or any other part of the premises of a harbour.
(2) The removal or destruction of goods under paragraph (1) and any loss of customs duties, rates or other charges incurred by it shall be at the expense of the consignee or other person concerned.”.

Repeal of regulations 57 and 58 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulations 57 and 58 of the principal Regulations are deleted.

Repeal and replacement of regulations 59 and 60 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulations 59 and 60 of the principal Regulations are deleted and the following substituted:

“Fumigation

  1. No ship may be fumigated in a harbour except with the written consent of the management and in accordance with the Immigration Act, Cap. 190.
    S.I. 2025 No. 84

Repairs to ships
60.(1) Except at authorised places, no structural repairs of ships may be made within a compulsory pilotage harbour except with the written permission of the management and subject to
(a)
the Merchant Shipping (Oil Pollution Prevention) Regulations, 2025 (S.I. 2025 No.22 );

(b)
the Merchant Shipping (Chemical Pollution Prevention) Regulations, 20254 (S.I. 2025 No.23 );

(c)
the Merchant Shipping (Sewage and Garbage Pollution Prevention) Regulations, 2024 (S.I. 2025 No.24 ); and

(d)
any other precautions that the management may direct to prevent dirt or other matter falling into the harbour.

(2) If the master or other person in charge of a ship contravenes paragraph (1), or fails to comply with the conditions of any permission granted, the permission to effect repairs may be withdrawn and the work stopped by the management.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 61 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Paragraph (1) of regulation 61 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Use of flame apparatus in harbour
61.(1) No construction, repair or maintenance work entailing the use of any hot-work, or any apparatus that produces extreme heat, shall be carried out on a ship in a compulsory pilotage harbour without the prior written permission of the management.”.
S.I. 2025 No. 84

Repeal and replacement of regulations 71 and 72 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulations 71 and 72 of the principal Regulations are deleted and the following substituted:

“Row boats to give way to sailing boats
71.(1) When a boat propelled by sails and another propelled by oars are proceeding on a course that, if continued, would involve the risk of collision, the vessels shall conduct themselves in accordance with the Convention on International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972, as amended.

Small craft to carry lights

  1. Small craft, when under way between sunset and sunrise, shall carry the lights prescribed by the Convention on International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972, as amended.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 78 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 78 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Certificate of fitness for small craft plying for hire
78.(1) A person who desires to ply for hire with, or let for hire, a tug, hulk, lighter, motor boat or other small craft shall apply to the management for a licence.
(2) On receipt of an application under paragraph (1), the management may appoint an inspector for the purpose of inspecting the craft.
S.I. 2025 No. 84
(3)
On an examination of the craft, if the inspector is of the opinion that the hull, equipment and machinery of the craft are in a suitable condition and fitted for the purpose and work for which they are intended, the inspector shall grant a certificate to that effect.

(4)
The certificate shall be valid for a period of 12 months from the day it is issued, unless previously cancelled, and shall state the purpose, whether the carriage of passengers or goods or both, for which the craft may be used and the number of persons or tonnage of goods or both she is licensed to carry.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 87 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 87 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Life-saving and fire extinguishing apparatus

  1. Every licensed small craft shall be equipped with lifesaving and fire-extinguishing appliances that are at all times fit and ready for use in accordance with the requirements of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, as amended.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 98 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 98 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Penalty for breach of small craft rules

  1. The owner or person in charge of a small craft licensed under regulation 79 who contravenes a regulation in this Part commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction, in addition to any other
    S.I. 2025 No. 84
    penalty to which he may be liable, to a fine of $20 000 or to imprisonment for a term of 2 months, or to both.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 101 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 101 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Suspension of licence for misconduct
101.(1) The management may suspend or revoke the licence of a small craft whose owner or any member of whose crew has breached a condition of the licence or has contravened a regulation in this Part or a lawful order of the management.
(2)
The management may require a licence referred to in paragraph

(1)
to be produced and any suspension or revocation shall be endorsed upon the licence.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 119 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 119 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Application
119.(1) Subject to paragraph (2), the regulations in this Part apply in respect of the processes of loading, unloading, moving and handling goods in or at a dock, wharf or quay, and the processes of loading and unloading a ship in a dock or harbour, but do not apply to the unloading of fish from a ship employed in the catching of fish.
(2) Regulations 122 to 131 do not apply to a small craft.”.
S.I. 2025 No. 84

Amendment of regulations 120 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Paragraphs (2) and (2A) of regulations 120 of the principal Regulations are deleted and the following substituted:
    “(2) The Chief Executive Officer of the Port may exempt the master of a ship registered in a country the Government of which is a party to the International Safety Convention from compliance with regulations 132 to 142 on proof that tests have been carried out in respect of the matters contained in those regulations.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 121 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 121(1) of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Appointment of persons to carry out tests and issue certificates
121.(1) For the purpose of regulations 132 to 134 and of regulation 137, the Chief Executive Officer of the Port may authorise such person to carry out any tests, examinations, inspections, annealing or other treatment that may be required in order to certify a certificate referred to in paragraph (2), and the Chief Executive Officer of the Port may at any time withdraw such an authorisation.
(1A) A person whose authorisation has been withdrawn may appeal the withdrawal to the Authority, whose decision shall be final.”.
S.I. 2025 No. 84
Amendment of regulation 122 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 122 of the principal Regulations is amended by
    (a) deleting the shoulder note and the chapeau of paragraph (1) and substituting the following:

“Safe means of access to berth
122.(1) If a ship is lying at a berth or quay for the purpose of loading or unloading or coaling, there shall be safe means of access for the use of persons employed at such times as they have to pass from the ship to the shore or from the shore to the ship as follows:”; and
(b) by deleting paragraph (3).

Repeal and replacement of regulation 124 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 124 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Safe means of access to other ships
124.(1) If a ship is alongside another ship and persons have to pass from one to the other, a safe means of access shall be provided for their use, unless the conditions are such that it is possible to pass from one to the other without undue risk without the aid of any special appliance.
(2) If one of the ships is a small craft of relatively low freeboard, the means of access shall be provided by the ship that has the higher freeboard.”.
S.I. 2025 No. 84

Repeal of regulation 127 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 127 of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal of regulation 129 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 129 of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal of regulation 131 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 131 of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 132 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 132 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following is substituted:

“Testing and examination of lifting machinery
132.(1) All lifting machinery shall, where practicable, be tested and examined by a person authorised by the Chief Executive Officer of the Port under regulation 121, in the manner set out in the Fourth Schedule, before being taken into use.
(2)
All cranes and permanent attachments, including bridle chains to a crane, mast and deck, used in hoisting or lowering shall be inspected once in every 12 months and be thoroughly examined once at least in every 4 years.

(3)
All other lifting machinery shall be thoroughly examined once at least in every 12 months.

(4)
For the purposes of this regulation “thorough examination” means a visual examination, supplemented if necessary by other means such as a hammer test, carried out as carefully as the conditions permit, in order to arrive at a reliable conclusion as to the safety of the parts

S.I. 2025 No. 84
examined, and, if necessary for the purpose, parts of the machines and gear shall be dismantled.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 133 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 133 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Testing of chains
133.(1) No chain, ring, hook, shackle, swivel or pulley block shall be used in hoisting or lowering unless it has been tested and examined by a person authorised by the Chief Executive Officer of the Port under regulation 121 as far as practicable in the manner set out in the Fourth Schedule.
(2)
All chains, other than bridle chains attached to cranes, derricks or masts, and all rings, hooks, shackles and swivels used in hoisting or lowering shall, unless they have been subjected to another treatment approved by the management, be effectually annealed under the supervision of a person authorised by the Chief Executive Officer of the Port under regulation 121 at the following intervals:

(a)
for half-inch and smaller chains, rings, hooks, shackles and swivels in general use, once at least in every 6 months; and

(b)
for all other chains, rings, hooks, shackles and swivels in general use, once at least in every 12 months.

(3)
Where the gear referred to in paragraph (2) is used solely on cranes and other hoisting appliances worked by hand, 12 months shall be substituted for 6 months in paragraph (2)(a) and 2 years for 12 months in paragraph (2)(b).

(4)
All chains, other than bridle chains attached to cranes, derricks or masts, and all rings, hooks, shackles, swivels and pulley blocks shall

S.I. 2025 No. 84
be inspected by a person authorised by the Chief Executive Officer of the Port under regulation 121 immediately before each occasion on which they are used in hoisting or lowering, unless they have been inspected within the preceding 3 months.
(5) All chains, rings, hooks, shackles or swivels used in hoisting or lowering that have been lengthened, altered or repaired by welding shall, before being again taken into use, be adequately tested and reexamined.”.

Repeal of regulation 137A of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 137A of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal of regulation 141 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 141 of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal of regulation 142 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 142 of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 143 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 143 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Escape of workers in a hold

  1. Precautions shall be taken to facilitate the escape of workers when employed in a hold or on tween docks in dealing with bulk cargo.”.
    S.I. 2025 No. 84

Repeal of regulation 145A of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 145A of the principal Regulations is deleted.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 145C of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 145C of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Provision of first-aid boxes
145C.(1) A sufficient number of first-aid boxes shall be provided at every working place and, if more than one is provided, at reasonable distances from each other.
(2)
A first-aid box shall be marked plainly with a white cross on a red background.

(3)
Nothing except appliances or requisites for first-aid shall be kept in a first-aid box.

(4)
A first-aid box shall be kept stocked and in good order, and shall be placed under the charge of a responsible person.

(5)
A person referred to in paragraph (4) shall be trained in first-aid and be readily available during working hours.”.

Repeal of regulations 147 to 150 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulations 147 to 150 of the principal Regulations are deleted.

Amendment of regulation 159B of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 159B of the principal Regulations is amended by deleting the words “General Manager” and substituting the words “Chief Executive Officer of the Port”.
    S.I. 2025 No. 84
    Amendment of regulation 159C of L.N. 11 of 1961
  2. Regulation 159C of the principal Regulations is amended by deleting the words “General Manager” and substituting the words “Chief Executive Officer of the Port”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 159D of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 159D of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:

“Report of accidents
159D. The Chief Executive Officer of the Port shall make to the Authority for transmission to the Minister a report, in such form and at such intervals as the Minister directs, of all accidents occurring in any harbour.”.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 161 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 161 of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following is substituted:

“Transit sheds.

  1. Subject to permission by an authorized official transit sheds shall be closed to members of the public, and no vehicle shall enter a transit shed without the authority of an authorised employee.”.
    Repeal of regulation 180 of L.N. 11 of 1961
  2. Regulation 180 of the principal Regulations is repealed.
    S.I. 2025 No. 84

  1. Regulation 183 of the principal Regulations is repealed.

Amendment of regulation 203 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Paragraphs (1) and (2) of regulation 203 of the principal Regulations are amended by deleting the words “General Manager” and substituting the words “Chief Executive Officer of the Port”.
  2. Regulation 205 of the principal Regulations is repealed.
  3. Regulation 206 of the principal Regulations is repealed.

Repeal and replacement of regulation 214C of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 214C of the principal Regulations is deleted and the following substituted:
    S.I. 2025 No. 84

“Definition of “harbour area”
214C. For the purposes of regulations 214A and 214B, “harbour area” means the area described in paragraphs (a) and (b) of the First Schedule to the Barbados Port Inc. (Transfer of Management and Vesting of Assets) Act, 2003, Cap. 285B.”.

Repeal of regulation 217 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 217 of the principal Regulations is repealed.

Repeal of regulation 218 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Regulation 218 of the principal Regulations is repealed.

Amendment of regulation 221 of L.N. 11 of 1961

  1. Paragraphs (1) and (2) of regulations 221 of the principal Regulations are deleted and the following substituted:
    “221.(1) Subject to regulation 120(2), the owner and master of a ship that does not comply with any of regulations 132 to 142 commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of $50 000 or to imprisonment for a term of 3 months or to both.
    (2) Every person who contravenes Part XI or a requirement in the Fifth Schedule commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of $50 000 or to imprisonment for a term of 3 months or to both.
